intro: Every ride on a skateboard is a science lesson on wheels. A foot pushes the ground, and the board starts to roll. A pebble stops a wheel, and the rider keeps going. A skater drops down a ramp, speeds up, then slows as she climbs the other side. Each of these moments has a cause you can name.

In this unit you will meet the forces that move a board: pushes, pulls, friction and gravity. You will learn about inertia and Isaac Newton's first law. Then you will follow energy as it trades from height to speed and back on a ramp, and see where some of it goes.

By the end, you will be able to explain why a board slows down, why soft wheels roll over cracks, and why a higher start means more speed. You will also know how to use a foot brake, how to fall small, and how skaters pump to keep going on a halfpipe.
bigQuestion: What forces and energy changes make a skateboard start, speed up, slow down and stop?

A skater's push starting a board rolling
A board sitting in a garage

test.why: The back foot brushes the ground, then presses gently to make friction and slow down.

test.why: Newton's first law, from the Principia of 1687, describes inertia.

test.why: Soft urethane wheels squish around bumps and grip the ground, so cracks stop them less.
On the durometer A scale, a lower number means a softer wheel.

test.why: Height gives her stored, or potential, energy. She is still, so she has no kinetic energy yet.

choices: Her stored energy becomes motion energy
Her motion energy turns into stored energy
test.why: Climbing, she slows down as motion energy turns back into stored energy.

test.why: A higher start stores more energy, which becomes more speed at the bottom.

Crouches into the curve and stands tall as it lifts her

tips: Name the energy at each spot: stored energy, motion energy, or both.
Say where she is fastest and why.
Explain where friction sends some energy: heat and sound.
Describe pumping step by step: crouch into the curve, stand tall as it lifts you.
Use at least four words from the unit, such as potential energy, kinetic energy, friction and transition.

title: Forces on Four Wheels

chapters.title: Push, Pull and Inertia
chapters.bigQuestion: What starts a skateboard rolling, what keeps it going, and what makes it stop?

story.title: The Board That Slowly Stopped
story.kicker: A fourth-grade class watches a board roll across the gym and asks a big question.
paragraphs: Mr. Ortiz sets a skateboard on the gym floor. Nobody is standing on it. The class sits in a half circle along the painted line. "Watch closely," he says. He gives the board one firm shove with his hand. It rolls across the shiny wood with a soft hum.
The board rolls past the free-throw line. Then it starts to slow down. It drifts past half court. At last it creeps to a stop near the far wall. Nobody touched it after that first shove.

Maya raises her hand. "Why did it stop? Nothing grabbed it." Leo has an idea. "Maybe it just ran out of push." Ana shakes her head. "I think the floor slowed it down. The wheels were rubbing on something."

Mr. Ortiz smiles and picks up the board. He spins one wheel with his finger. It whirs, then slows, then stops. "Something is working on this wheel," he says. "Today we find out what it is." He writes three words on the whiteboard: push, inertia, friction.
story.think: Leo said the board ran out of push. Ana said the floor slowed it down. Which idea do you think is closer, and why?

lessons.title: A Force Is a Push or a Pull
lessons.mainIdea: A force is a push or a pull, and every force has a size and a direction.
reading: Stand on a skateboard with your front foot over the front bolts. Put your back foot on the ground. Press back against the ground. The board rolls forward. Your foot gave a *push*. A push presses something away from you. A push is one kind of *force*.

A *pull* is a force too. A pull brings something toward you. Hook your toe under the nose of a resting board and lift. The nose tips up toward you. Tug a board along by a rope, and you are pulling it. Every force is either a push or a pull.

Every force has a size and a direction. A gentle push starts the board slowly. A strong push starts it faster. Your back foot pushes backward on the ground. The ground pushes you forward in return. That is why a push off the ground moves you ahead.

words.d: a push or a pull on something
a force that presses something away from you
a force that brings something toward you

look.title: The First Push of a Ride
look.text: Picture a skater with a buckled helmet on a smooth, empty playground. Her front foot rests over the front bolts. Her back foot steps down beside the board. It presses back on the ground and lifts away. The board glides ahead. She sets her back foot on the board over the back bolts and rolls.
look.prompt: Which way does her back foot push the ground? Which way does the board go?

check.q: What is a force?
choices: The rough top of a deck
check.why: A force is a push or a pull. Pushes and pulls make things start, stop or change direction.

check.q: Lifting the nose of a board up toward you with your toe is what kind of force?
check.why: A pull brings something toward you. Lifting the nose toward you is a pull.

check.q: When your back foot pushes backward on the ground, which way do you move?
check.why: Your foot pushes back on the ground, and the ground pushes you forward in return.

lessons.title: Balanced and Unbalanced Forces
lessons.mainIdea: Balanced forces cancel out and nothing changes; an unbalanced force changes how a board moves.
reading: A skateboard sits on a flat driveway. Gravity pulls it down. The ground pushes it up just as hard. The two forces are the same size. They point in opposite directions. They cancel each other out. These are *balanced forces*. The board stays still.

Now a skater steps on and pushes off. The push forward is bigger than anything pushing back. That is an *unbalanced force*. An unbalanced force changes motion. It can start a board, speed it up, slow it down or turn it.

Think of a tug-of-war. If both teams pull equally hard, the rope does not move. If one team pulls harder, the rope moves toward that team. A board works the same way. Only an unbalanced force makes its motion change.

words.d: forces that are equal in size and opposite in direction, so they cancel out
a force that is not canceled out, so it changes how something moves

look.title: Two Boards Side by Side
look.text: Board A sits still on the floor. Gravity pulls it down. The floor pushes it up the same amount. Board B rolls along. A skater's foot just pushed it forward, harder than anything holding it back. Draw two arrows on Board A that point opposite ways and are the same length. Draw one long arrow on Board B pointing forward.
look.prompt: Which board has balanced forces? Which one has an unbalanced force?

check.q: A board sits still on a flat floor. What is true about the forces on it?
choices: There are no forces on it
Only the floor pushes on it
check.why: Gravity pulls down and the floor pushes up just as hard, so the forces are balanced and the board stays still.

check.q: What does an unbalanced force do?
check.why: An unbalanced force changes motion. It can start, speed up, slow down or turn a board.

check.q: In a tug-of-war, both teams pull equally hard. What happens to the rope?
check.why: Equal pulls in opposite directions are balanced forces, so the rope does not move.

lessons.title: What Inertia Means
lessons.mainIdea: Inertia means things keep doing what they are doing until a force makes them change.
reading: A skateboard rests in the corner of a garage. It will sit there all week. It will not start rolling on its own. Something has to push or pull it first. Things that are still tend to stay still. That is one half of *inertia*.

Inertia has a second half. Things that are moving tend to keep moving. They keep the same speed and go in a straight line. Something has to push or pull to slow them, stop them or turn them. Inertia is not a force. It is how every object acts.

Heavier things have more inertia. An empty shopping cart is easy to start and easy to stop. A full cart is harder to start and harder to stop. A grown-up on a board is harder to stop than a small child at the same speed.

words.d: the way an object keeps doing what it is doing, staying still or moving the same way, until a force changes it
moving from one place to another

look.title: The Coin on the Card
look.text: Lay a playing card on top of a cup. Set a coin in the middle of the card. Flick the card hard and fast, straight sideways. The card shoots away. The coin does not go with it. It drops straight down into the cup. The coin was still, and it stayed still.
look.prompt: How does the coin show inertia? What would happen if you pulled the card slowly?

check.q: A board rests in a garage. What will it do if nothing pushes or pulls it?
check.why: Things that are still tend to stay still. That is inertia.

check.q: Which statement about inertia is true?
choices: Inertia is a kind of push
Moving things tend to keep moving
check.why: Inertia has two halves: still things stay still, and moving things keep moving until a force changes them.

check.q: Which is harder to stop at the same speed?
choices: A small child on a board
check.why: Heavier things have more inertia, so a grown-up is harder to stop than a small child at the same speed.

lessons.title: The Pebble Stop
lessons.mainIdea: When a wheel hits a pebble, the board stops but your body keeps going forward because of inertia.
reading: A rider rolls along a path. A front wheel hits a small rock. The rock pushes back hard on the wheel. The board stops almost at once. But nothing pushed back on the rider's body. Inertia keeps the body moving forward. The rider steps or tumbles off the front.

This is why skaters scan the ground ahead. Look for pebbles, sticks and cracks before you reach them. A helmet that fits and is buckled protects your head. Wrist guards and knee pads protect the places that hit the ground most often.

If you do fall, fall small. First, bend your knees and get low. Next, tuck your chin. Then roll onto your side or slide on your knee pads. Do not catch yourself with straight, locked arms. Locked arms can hurt your wrists.

words.d: the way a moving body keeps moving until a force stops it
to get low, tuck and roll so a fall is short and soft

look.title: Board Stops, Rider Goes
look.text: Picture a rider rolling at walking speed. The front wheels bump a pebble. The board stops in place. The rider's body still leans and moves forward. She runs off the nose for two quick steps. Because she was going slowly, she stays on her feet.
look.prompt: Why did the rider keep moving when the board stopped? How did going slowly help her?

check.q: A front wheel hits a pebble and the board stops. Why does the rider keep going forward?
check.why: Nothing pushed back on the rider's body, so inertia kept it moving forward.

check.q: When you fall, what should you do with your arms?
choices: Lock them straight to catch yourself
check.why: Do not catch yourself with straight, locked arms. Get low, tuck and roll instead.

check.q: What is the first step in falling small?
choices: Bend your knees and get low
check.why: First you bend your knees and get low. Then you tuck your chin and roll or slide.

lessons.title: Friction Slows the Board
lessons.mainIdea: Friction is a force between two surfaces that rub, and it slowly stops a rolling board.
reading: Remember the board in the gym. It slowed down and stopped with nobody touching it. A force did that. The force is *friction*. Friction happens when two surfaces rub or press together. It works against motion.

A rolling board has friction in more than one place. The wheels press and flex against the floor. The *bearings* inside the wheels rub a little as they spin. The air pushes on the board and rider. Each one takes away a bit of speed.

Smooth surfaces make less friction than rough ones. A board rolls far on a smooth gym floor. It rolls a shorter way on bumpy blacktop. It stops quickly in grass. Friction is why the board needs another push to keep going.

words.d: a force between two surfaces that rub or press together; it works against motion
small rings of steel balls inside each wheel that let it spin smoothly

look.title: How Far One Push Goes
look.cite: Example numbers to show the pattern; real distances depend on the push, the board and the wheels
look.prompt: Which surface made the most friction? How can you tell from the numbers?

check.q: What force slowed the board in the gym?
choices: A push from the air conditioner
check.why: Friction between surfaces works against motion. It slowed the board until it stopped.

check.q: Where does friction act on a rolling board?
choices: In the wheels, the bearings and the air
check.why: The wheels on the ground, the bearings inside the wheels and the air all add friction.

check.q: On which surface would a board roll the shortest distance?
check.why: Grass is rough and soft, so it makes the most friction and stops the board quickly.

lessons.title: Friction You Want
lessons.mainIdea: Friction is also helpful: it keeps your shoes on the deck and lets your foot slow the board.
reading: Look at the top of a deck. It is covered in *grip tape*. Grip tape is rough, like sandpaper. It makes lots of friction with the soles of your shoes. That friction keeps your feet from sliding off. Flat shoes with grippy soles help even more.

Friction also helps you stop. One way is the foot brake. First, keep your front foot over the front bolts, pointing forward. Next, bend your front knee. Then lower your back foot and let the sole touch the ground lightly. Press a little harder to slow more.

A common problem is stomping the back foot down too hard. The shoe grabs and you lurch forward. The fix is to brush the ground first, then press slowly. Practice the foot brake at walking speed on flat, smooth ground away from cars.

words.d: rough, sandpaper-like sheet on top of the deck that keeps shoes from slipping
slowing down by dragging the sole of the back foot lightly on the ground

look.title: The Foot Brake, Step by Step
look.text: Step 1: Roll slowly with both feet on the board. Step 2: Turn your front foot so it points forward over the front bolts. Step 3: Bend your front knee so your weight stays on the board. Step 4: Lower your back foot and brush the ground with your whole sole. Step 5: Press gently until you stop.
look.prompt: Which foot stays on the board, and which foot makes the friction?

check.q: Why is grip tape rough?
choices: To make the board roll faster
To make friction that keeps shoes from slipping
check.why: Rough grip tape makes friction with your soles, so your feet stay on the deck.

check.q: In a foot brake, which foot touches the ground?
check.why: The front foot stays over the front bolts. The back foot brushes the ground to make friction.

check.q: You stomp your back foot down and lurch forward. What is the fix?
choices: Brush the ground first, then press slowly
check.why: Brushing first and pressing slowly lets friction build up smoothly instead of grabbing all at once.

lessons.title: Gravity Pulls Everything Down
lessons.mainIdea: Gravity is a pull toward the center of the Earth that acts on everything, all the time.
reading: Drop a skateboard wheel and a pencil. Both fall to the floor. Something pulled them down. That pull is *gravity*. Gravity pulls everything toward the center of the Earth. It never turns off.

Gravity keeps a skater pressed onto the deck. When a skater hops, gravity pulls her back down. The strength of gravity's pull on your body is your *weight*. A heavier rider is pulled down harder than a lighter one.

Gravity also pulls a board down a slope. On a hill, part of the pull points downhill. The board speeds up even without a push. That is why beginners stay on flat ground. Practice slowing down before you try even a gentle slope, with a grown-up nearby.

words.d: the pull that draws everything toward the center of the Earth
how hard gravity pulls down on something

look.title: Flat Ground and a Gentle Slope
look.text: Board A sits on a flat path. Gravity pulls straight down, and the path pushes straight up. Board A stays put. Board B sits on a gentle slope. Gravity still pulls straight down, but now the ground is tilted. Board B starts to roll downhill by itself.
look.prompt: Why does Board B roll but Board A does not? Which force is the same for both?

check.q: Which way does gravity pull?
choices: Toward the center of the Earth
check.why: Gravity pulls everything toward the center of the Earth, which we feel as down.

check.q: What is weight?
choices: How hard gravity pulls on you
check.why: Weight is the strength of gravity's pull on your body.

check.q: Why does a board roll down a slope without a push?
choices: Part of gravity's pull points downhill
check.why: On a tilted surface, part of gravity's pull points downhill, so the board speeds up.

lessons.title: Newton's First Law
lessons.mainIdea: Newton's first law says an object stays still or keeps moving straight at the same speed unless a force changes it.
reading: Isaac Newton was an English scientist. In 1687 he published a famous book called the *Principia*. In it, he wrote three laws of motion. The first one describes inertia. People call it *Newton's first law*.

Here it is in plain words. A still object stays still. A moving object keeps moving at the same speed in a straight line. Both stay that way until an unbalanced force acts on them. A force is needed to change motion, not to keep it going.

A skateboard shows the law every day. On a perfectly smooth floor with no air, one push would send a board on and on. On real ground, friction is always acting. Friction is the force that changes the board's motion and stops it.

words.d: an object stays still or keeps moving straight at the same speed unless an unbalanced force acts on it
Isaac Newton's book of 1687 that set out his laws of motion

look.title: Newton's First Law, in Newton's Book
look.text: Every body keeps on resting, or keeps on moving evenly in a straight line, unless forces pressed on it make it change.
look.cite: Isaac Newton, Principia (1687; Andrew Motte's English translation, 1729), Law I, in plain words
look.prompt: What does Newton say it takes to change how something moves?

check.q: In what year did Newton publish the Principia?
check.why: Newton published the Principia, with his laws of motion, in 1687.

check.q: According to Newton's first law, what keeps a rolling board from rolling forever?
check.why: A force is needed to change motion. Friction is the force that slows and stops the board.

check.q: Newton's first law says a force is needed to do what?
check.why: A force is needed to change motion, not to keep it going or keep a still object still.

lessons.title: Soft Wheels Roll Over Cracks
lessons.mainIdea: Soft urethane wheels squeeze around small bumps and grip the ground, so cracks and pebbles stop them less.
reading: Early skateboards had clay or steel wheels. They were hard and slick. A small pebble could stop a steel wheel cold. Then the rider's inertia carried him forward off the board. In the early 1970s, *urethane* wheels changed this. Urethane is a tough, rubbery plastic.

A soft urethane wheel squishes a little when it meets a bump. It wraps around a small pebble or the edge of a crack. The bump pushes back on the wheel more gently. The board slows less, and it keeps rolling. The ride also feels smoother and quieter.

Soft wheels also grip better. More of the wheel presses on the ground, so there is more friction sideways. That grip helps the board turn without sliding out. Riders on rough streets often pick softer wheels. Hard wheels feel faster on very smooth skatepark floors.

words.d: a tough, rubbery plastic used to make skateboard wheels since the early 1970s
how well a wheel holds the ground without sliding

look.title: Two Wheels Meet One Crack
look.text: Picture two boards rolling side by side toward the same crack in the sidewalk. Board A has hard steel wheels. Board B has soft urethane wheels. Board A's wheel bangs into the edge and stops. Board B's wheel squishes over the edge, bounces a tiny bit, and rolls on.
look.prompt: Why did the soft wheel keep rolling? What would the rider of Board A feel?

check.q: When did urethane wheels change skateboarding?
check.why: Urethane wheels came in the early 1970s and replaced slick clay and steel wheels.

check.q: Why does a soft wheel roll over a small pebble more easily?
choices: It squishes and wraps around the bump
check.why: A soft wheel squishes around the pebble, so the bump pushes back on it more gently.

check.q: Why do soft wheels help a board turn without sliding out?
check.why: More of a soft wheel presses on the ground, which gives more sideways friction, or grip.

lessons.title: Measuring Wheel Hardness
lessons.mainIdea: Wheel hardness is measured with a durometer; smaller numbers mean softer wheels.
reading: Turn over a skateboard wheel. Look on its side. You may see a number and a letter, such as 78A or 99A. That label tells how hard the wheel is. Hardness is measured with a tool called a *durometer*.

A durometer presses a small, blunt pin into the wheel. A soft wheel lets the pin sink in more. A hard wheel pushes back and lets the pin sink in less. The tool shows a number. Most skateboard wheels are measured on the A scale.

On the A scale, a lower number means a softer wheel. Soft wheels are about 78A. They roll smoothly over cracks and grip well. Hard wheels are about 99A to 101A. They slide more easily, which some skaters want for slides on smooth concrete.

words.d: a tool that measures how hard a material is by pressing a small pin into it
how much a material resists being pressed in

look.title: Example Wheel Hardness Numbers
look.cite: Typical durometer A values for skateboard wheels (examples; brands vary)
look.prompt: Which wheel would roll most smoothly over a cracked sidewalk? How do you know?

check.q: What tool measures wheel hardness?
check.why: A durometer presses a small pin into a wheel to measure how hard it is.

check.q: On the A scale, which wheel is softest?
check.why: On the A scale, a lower number means a softer wheel, so 78A is the softest.

check.q: Why might a skater choose a very hard wheel?
choices: To slide more easily on smooth concrete
To grip better on rough streets
check.why: Hard wheels, about 99A to 101A, slide more easily, which some skaters want for slides.

review.q: Which of these is a pull?
choices: Pressing back on the ground with your foot
Lifting the nose of a board toward you
review.why: A pull brings something toward you. Lifting the nose toward you is a pull.

review.q: A board sits still on flat ground. What is true?
choices: The forces on it are balanced
review.why: Gravity pulls down and the ground pushes up equally, so the forces are balanced.

choices: The way things keep doing what they are doing until a force changes them
The rough top of a deck
review.why: Inertia is how objects stay still or keep moving until a force changes them. It is not a force.

review.q: Why does a rider fly forward when a wheel hits a rock?
choices: The rider's body keeps moving because of inertia
review.why: The rock stops the board, but nothing stops the rider's body, so inertia carries it forward.

review.q: What does friction do to a rolling board?
review.why: Friction works against motion, so it slows a rolling board and finally stops it.

review.q: In a foot brake, where does the front foot stay?
choices: Over the front bolts, pointing forward
review.why: The front foot stays over the front bolts, pointing forward, while the back foot brushes the ground.

review.q: What does Newton's first law say?
choices: An object keeps its motion unless an unbalanced force changes it
review.why: Newton's first law says still things stay still and moving things keep moving straight unless a force acts.

review.q: A wheel is labeled 78A. What does that tell you?
review.why: On the durometer A scale, about 78A is a soft wheel that grips and rolls over cracks.

chapters.title: Energy on a Ramp
chapters.bigQuestion: Where does a skater's speed on a ramp come from, and where does it go?

story.title: The Marble in the Bowl
story.kicker: A marble rolls back and forth in a bowl, and each trip is a little lower.
paragraphs: Ms. Patel holds up a large, round salad bowl. She sets it on a table at the front of the room. Then she holds a glass marble against the inside rim. "Watch where it goes," she says. She lets go without pushing.

The marble races down the curved side. It zips across the bottom. It climbs the far side and almost reaches the rim. Then it stops for a split second and rolls back. Back and forth it goes, with a soft clicking sound.

Jordan leans in close. "It is not going as high now," he says. He is right. Each trip ends a little lower on the side of the bowl. After many trips, the marble rocks gently at the bottom. At last it sits still.

"This bowl is like a halfpipe at a skatepark," Ms. Patel says. "A skater rolls up one wall and down the other, just like the marble." Sofia frowns. "Then why do skaters not stop at the bottom too?" Ms. Patel grins. "That," she says, "is today's question."
story.think: The marble never rolled higher than where it started. Why do you think each trip was a little lower?

lessons.title: Height Stores Energy
lessons.mainIdea: Anything lifted up high has stored energy, called potential energy, that gravity can turn into motion.
reading: A skater carries her board up the steps to the deck of a small ramp. The deck is the flat top at the edge. Up there, she is not moving. But she has something she did not have at the bottom. She has stored energy from being high up.

*Energy* is the ability to make things move or change. Energy stored in something lifted up is called *potential energy*. Potential means ready to happen. Gravity is ready to pull the skater down. When it does, the stored energy will turn into speed.

The higher something is, the more energy it stores. A board on the deck of a tall ramp has more stored energy than one on a short ramp. A heavier rider at the same height also stores more. Height and weight both add stored energy.

words.d: the ability to make things move or change
stored energy; for a skater, energy stored by being high up

look.title: Three Balls on Three Shelves
look.text: Picture three tennis balls. One sits on a low step. One sits on a table. One sits on a high shelf. Each one is still. Now picture each ball falling to the floor. The one from the high shelf hits hardest and bounces highest.
look.prompt: Which ball had the most stored energy before it fell? What gave it that energy?

check.q: What is potential energy?
choices: The energy of a spinning wheel
Stored energy, such as from being high up
The rough feel of grip tape
check.why: Potential energy is stored energy. A skater high on a ramp has stored energy from the height.

check.q: Which skater stores more energy?
choices: The same rider on a short ramp
The same rider on flat ground
The same rider on a tall ramp
check.why: The higher something is, the more energy it stores. The tall ramp gives the most.

check.q: What does the word potential mean?
check.why: Potential means ready to happen. Stored energy is ready to turn into motion.

lessons.title: Lifting Takes Energy
lessons.mainIdea: Energy is never made from nothing; a skater's muscles supply the energy that gets stored as height.
reading: Climbing to the top of a ramp takes effort. Your legs work hard. You may breathe faster. Your muscles are using energy from the food you ate. Some of that energy gets stored in your body as height.

Energy does not appear out of nothing. It also does not vanish. It changes from one form to another. Food energy becomes muscle energy. Muscle energy lifts you and becomes stored energy. Scientists call this idea *conservation of energy*.

This is why the top of the ramp is a kind of energy bank. You put energy in by climbing up or by pushing hard to roll up. Gravity lets you take it back out as speed. You can only take out what you put in.

words.d: the rule that energy is never made or destroyed; it only changes form
a kind of energy, such as stored, motion, heat or sound energy

look.title: Follow the Energy
look.text: A boy eats a banana at lunch. After school, he carries his skateboard up the steps to the deck of a low ramp. Follow the energy: the banana gives his body food energy. His leg muscles use it to lift him and the board. At the top, the energy is stored in his height.
look.prompt: Name the forms the energy took, in order, from the banana to the top of the ramp.

check.q: Where does the energy to climb a ramp come from?
choices: From the food your muscles use
check.why: Your muscles use energy from food to lift you. That energy is then stored as height.

check.q: What does conservation of energy mean?
choices: Energy changes form but is never made or destroyed
check.why: Conservation of energy means energy only changes from one form to another.

check.q: Why can a skater only get out as much speed as the energy put in?
choices: Energy cannot be made from nothing
check.why: Energy does not appear out of nothing, so the speed you get out comes from energy you put in.

lessons.title: Motion Energy
lessons.mainIdea: Anything that is moving has motion energy, called kinetic energy, and faster things have more.
reading: A rolling board can knock over a cone. A still board cannot. The rolling board has energy because it is moving. Energy of motion is called *kinetic energy*. The word kinetic comes from a Greek word about moving.

Speed matters a lot for kinetic energy. A board rolling fast has much more motion energy than the same board rolling slowly. That is why a fast fall hurts more than a slow one. More energy has to go somewhere when you stop.

Weight matters too. A grown-up rolling at walking speed has more motion energy than a small child at the same speed. *Speed* is how far something goes in a certain time. Faster and heavier both mean more kinetic energy.

words.d: the energy something has because it is moving
how far something goes in a certain amount of time

look.title: Two Boards and a Cone
look.text: Two boards roll toward two plastic cones. Board A rolls slowly, at a crawl. It bumps its cone, which wobbles but stays up. Board B rolls fast. It hits its cone and sends it tumbling across the playground.
look.prompt: Which board had more kinetic energy? What clue tells you?

check.q: What is kinetic energy?
check.why: Kinetic energy is the energy something has because it is moving.

check.q: Which has the most kinetic energy?
choices: A still board on a high deck
check.why: Faster means more kinetic energy. A still board has no kinetic energy at all.

check.q: Why does a fast fall hurt more than a slow one?
choices: There is more motion energy to stop
Gravity is stronger when you are fast
check.why: A fast rider has much more kinetic energy, and all of it has to go somewhere when you stop.

lessons.title: The Big Energy Trade
lessons.mainIdea: Rolling down a ramp trades stored energy for motion energy; rolling up trades it back.
reading: A skater stands on the deck of a small ramp. She has lots of stored energy and no motion energy. She rolls down the curved wall. As she gets lower, she goes faster. Her stored energy is turning into motion energy.
At the bottom of the ramp, she is at her lowest point. She is also at her fastest. Almost all of her stored energy has become kinetic energy. The flat part at the bottom is called the *flat bottom*.

Now she rolls up the other wall. She slows down as she climbs. Her motion energy turns back into stored energy. At the top she stops for a moment. This back-and-forth change is an *energy trade*. Gravity does the trading.

words.d: energy changing from one form to another and back, like stored energy to motion energy
the flat part at the bottom of a ramp between the curved walls

look.title: Four Spots on a Ramp
look.text: Picture a skater at four spots. Spot 1: on top of the deck, still. Spot 2: halfway down the wall, picking up speed. Spot 3: on the flat bottom, rolling fastest. Spot 4: high on the far wall, slowing almost to a stop.
look.prompt: At which spot does she have the most stored energy? At which spot does she have the most motion energy?

check.q: Where on a ramp is a skater fastest?
choices: At the very top of the far wall
check.why: At the lowest point, almost all stored energy has become motion energy, so she is fastest there.

check.q: Rolling up a ramp wall changes which energy into which?
check.why: Climbing slows the skater as her motion energy turns back into stored energy.

check.q: What does the trading of energy on a ramp?
check.why: Gravity pulls the skater down to speed her up and slows her on the way up.

lessons.title: A Ramp Works Like a Slide
lessons.mainIdea: A ramp works like a playground slide: gravity pulls you along the slope, and a curve turns falling into rolling.
reading: Think about a playground slide. You climb the ladder. You sit at the top. Then gravity pulls you down the slope, faster and faster. A skate ramp works the same way. The board is like you, and the curved wall is like the slide.

A ramp's curved wall is called a *transition*. It goes from steep near the top to flat at the bottom. The curve guides the board. It turns the drop into forward rolling. Without the curve, the board would hit the ground hard.

A slide has a ladder. A ramp may have steps up to its deck. Either way, you use your muscles to get to the top. The ride down gives you back that energy as speed. Ride only ramps sized for beginners, with pads and a buckled helmet.

words.d: a sloped or curved surface that skaters roll up and down
the curved part of a ramp that goes from steep to flat

look.title: Slide and Ramp Side by Side
look.text: On the left, a girl sits at the top of a curly playground slide. On the right, a boy stands on the deck of a small quarter pipe ramp. Both are high up. Both are still. When they go, both pick up speed on the way down. Both curves end flat at the bottom.
look.prompt: Name two ways the slide and the ramp are alike. Name one way they are different.

check.q: What is the transition on a ramp?
choices: The curved part from steep to flat
check.why: The transition is the curved wall that goes from steep near the top to flat at the bottom.

check.q: How is a ramp like a playground slide?
choices: Gravity pulls you down both and you speed up
Both slow you down on the way down
check.why: On both, you climb up using your muscles, and gravity pulls you down the slope faster and faster.

check.q: What does the curve of a ramp do?
choices: Turns the drop into forward rolling
check.why: The curve guides the board from going down to rolling forward, so it does not hit the ground hard.

lessons.title: A Higher Start Gives More Speed
lessons.mainIdea: The higher a skater starts, the more stored energy there is, so the faster the skater goes at the bottom.
reading: Two friends try the same idea at a skatepark. One starts at the top of a small bank. The other starts at the top of a taller bank. They roll down without pushing. The rider from the taller bank is going faster at the bottom.

A higher start stores more energy. More stored energy turns into more motion energy at the bottom. More motion energy means more speed. So height buys speed. That is why big ramps are for skaters with lots of practice.

The speed does not grow as fast as the height, though. A ramp twice as tall does not make you twice as fast. It still makes you faster every time. Scientists can figure out the speed from the height. The chart shows some *worked example* numbers.

words.d: numbers figured out step by step to show how an idea works
a flat, tilted ramp with no curve

look.title: Speed at the Bottom From Different Heights
look.unit: meters per second at the bottom
look.cite: Worked example with g = 9.8 m/s², with no friction; real speeds are a little lower
look.prompt: The 2.0 m start is four times as high as the 0.5 m start. Is the speed four times as fast?

check.q: Two riders roll down without pushing. Who is faster at the bottom?
choices: The one from the short bank
The one from the taller bank
check.why: A higher start stores more energy, which becomes more speed at the bottom.

check.q: If a ramp is twice as tall, what happens to the speed at the bottom?
choices: It is faster, but not twice as fast
It is exactly twice as fast
check.why: Speed does not grow as fast as height. A taller ramp makes you faster, but not twice as fast.

check.q: In the chart, about how fast is a rider from a 1.0 m start?
check.why: The worked example shows about 4.4 meters per second from a 1.0 meter start, with no friction.

lessons.title: Rolling Up and Back on a Bank
lessons.mainIdea: On a low bank, gravity slows you as you roll up and speeds you up as you roll back down.
reading: A low bank is a good first ramp. Wear a buckled helmet, wrist guards and pads, and have a grown-up nearby. First, push slowly toward the bank on flat ground. Keep your front foot over the front bolts and your back foot over the back bolts. Bend your knees.

Next, roll a short way up the bank. Feel the board slow down. Gravity is trading your motion energy for stored energy. Keep your weight centered between your feet. As you stop, turn your head to look back down the bank.

Then let the board roll backward down the bank. Riding backward with your feet in your normal stance is called *fakie*. Stay low and centered. A common problem is leaning back toward the bank, so the board slips out. The fix is to keep your weight over the board, not behind it.

words.d: rolling backward while standing in your normal stance
with your weight in the middle of the board, between both feet

look.title: Up, Pause, Back
look.text: Step 1: Roll slowly toward a low bank, knees bent. Step 2: Ride a short way up. Step 3: Feel the board slow and stop. Step 4: Turn your head to look down the bank. Step 5: Roll back down fakie, low and centered. Step 6: Ride away on flat ground.
look.prompt: At which step is your stored energy highest? At which step does it turn back into speed?

check.q: Why does a board slow down as it rolls up a bank?
choices: Gravity trades motion energy for stored energy
The grip tape grabs the ground
check.why: Rolling up, gravity slows the board as motion energy turns into stored energy.

check.q: What is fakie?
choices: Rolling backward in your normal stance
check.why: Fakie means rolling backward while standing in your normal stance.

check.q: Your board slips out when you roll back down. What is the likely fix?
choices: Keep your weight over the board, not behind it
Stand up straight with stiff knees
check.why: Leaning back toward the bank makes the board slip out. Keeping your weight centered over the board fixes it.

lessons.title: Friction Turns Motion Into Heat
lessons.mainIdea: Friction changes some motion energy into heat and sound, so a rolling board loses energy over time.
reading: Rub your hands together fast. They get warm. The rubbing is friction. Friction changed the motion of your hands into *heat*. A rolling skateboard does the same thing, only more slowly.

Each time a wheel squishes against the ground, a little energy turns to heat. The bearings warm up a tiny bit as they spin. The wheels make a rolling sound. *Sound energy* is energy too. The air pushes against the rider and takes some energy away.

None of this energy is destroyed. It just spreads out as heat and sound. The heat and sound cannot easily turn back into speed. So the board has less motion energy than before. Every ride slowly hands energy over to the world around it.

words.d: energy that makes things warmer; friction turns motion into heat
energy carried by sound, such as the hum of rolling wheels

look.title: Feel the Warm Wheel
look.text: A skater rolls back and forth on a ramp for ten minutes. Then she stops and flips the board over. She touches a wheel with her fingertip. It feels a little warmer than when she started. She hears no rolling sound now, because the board is still.
look.prompt: Where did some of her motion energy go? What two clues does the story give?

check.q: What does friction turn some motion energy into?
check.why: Friction changes some motion energy into heat and sound.

check.q: Why do your hands get warm when you rub them fast?
check.why: Rubbing is friction, and friction changes motion energy into heat.

check.q: Is energy destroyed by friction?
choices: No, it turns into more speed
No, it spreads out as heat and sound
check.why: Energy is never destroyed. Friction spreads it out as heat and sound that cannot easily become speed again.

lessons.title: Never Quite as High
lessons.mainIdea: Because friction takes a little energy each trip, a rolling thing never climbs back quite as high as it started.
reading: Think back to the marble in the bowl. It started at the rim. It never rolled higher than the rim. Each trip ended a little lower. That pattern tells us energy was leaving the marble every trip.

Each time the marble rolled, friction and air took a small share of its energy. That share turned into heat and sound. Less energy was left for climbing. So the next trip was lower. After many trips, almost no motion energy was left, and the marble stopped.

A skater on a ramp works the same way. If she rolls without adding energy, each wall she reaches is a little lower. She can never roll higher than where she began. To keep going, she has to add energy with her own legs.

words.d: something that repeats in a way you can predict
energy leaving a moving thing as heat and sound, so it has less left for motion

look.title: How High the Marble Climbs Each Trip
look.unit: centimeters up the side of the bowl
look.cite: Example numbers to show the pattern; a real bowl and marble will give different heights
look.prompt: What happens to the height each trip? Could the marble ever climb back to 20 centimeters on its own?

check.q: Why does the marble climb a little lower each trip?
choices: Friction and air take a little energy each trip
check.why: Friction and air take a small share of energy each trip, so less is left for climbing.

check.q: Can a skater who adds no energy roll higher than where she started?
choices: Only if her wheels are hard
check.why: Energy is never made from nothing, and friction takes some, so she cannot climb higher than her start.

check.q: In the example chart, how high did the marble climb after trip 2?
check.why: The chart shows 15 centimeters after trip 2, lower than the 20 centimeters it started at.

lessons.title: The Halfpipe Energy Trade
lessons.mainIdea: On a halfpipe, energy trades back and forth between height and speed, and pumping with the legs adds the energy friction takes.
reading: A *halfpipe* is a U-shaped ramp. It has two curved walls facing each other and a flat bottom between them. A skater rolls up one wall, comes back down, crosses the bottom and rolls up the other wall. Energy trades from height to speed and back again.

Like the marble, a skater loses a little energy each trip. So how do skaters keep going? They *pump*. Pumping means bending low on the way into the curve, then standing up tall as the curve lifts you. The legs push, and that push adds energy.

Good pumping can add more energy than friction takes. Then each trip goes a little higher. That answers Sofia's question: the skater does not stop because her legs keep adding energy. Learners practice pumping on a small ramp first, low and slow.

words.d: a U-shaped ramp with two curved walls facing each other
to bend low into a curve and stand tall as it lifts you, adding energy with your legs

look.title: Pumping Across the Halfpipe
look.text: Picture a skater rolling down one wall of a small halfpipe. As she reaches the curve near the bottom, she bends her knees and crouches low. As the curve starts to lift her up the far wall, she stands up tall and pushes through her legs. She climbs a little higher than on her last trip.
look.prompt: When does she crouch, and when does she stand? Where does the extra energy come from?

check.q: What is a halfpipe?
choices: A U-shaped ramp with two curved walls
check.why: A halfpipe is a U-shaped ramp with two curved walls facing each other and a flat bottom.

check.q: When pumping, what does a skater do as the curve lifts her?
check.why: She bends low going into the curve and stands up tall as the curve lifts her, adding energy.

check.q: Why can a skater who pumps keep going on a halfpipe?
choices: Her legs add energy to replace what friction takes
check.why: Pumping adds energy with her legs, which can replace or beat the energy friction takes.

review.q: A skater stands still on top of a ramp. What kind of energy does she have most of?
review.why: Being high up gives her stored, or potential, energy. She is not moving, so she has no kinetic energy.

review.q: What happens to a skater's energy as she rolls down a ramp?
choices: Stored energy turns into motion energy
Motion energy turns into stored energy
review.why: Rolling down, stored energy from height turns into motion energy, so she speeds up.

review.q: Where is a skater fastest on a halfpipe?
choices: At the top of a wall
review.why: At the lowest point, the most stored energy has turned into motion energy.

review.q: Why does a higher start give more speed at the bottom?
choices: There is less friction up high
review.why: More height stores more energy, and that energy becomes more speed at the bottom.

review.q: What is the curved part of a ramp called?
review.why: The transition is the curved wall that goes from steep to flat.

review.q: Why does the marble in the bowl climb lower each trip?
choices: Friction turns some energy into heat and sound
review.why: Friction and air take a little energy each trip as heat and sound, leaving less for climbing.

review.q: What does conservation of energy say?
choices: Energy changes form but is never made or destroyed
review.why: Energy only changes from one form to another. It is never made from nothing or destroyed.

review.q: How does pumping help a skater on a halfpipe?
choices: Her legs add energy each trip
review.why: Bending low and standing tall in the curve lets her legs add energy to replace what friction takes.
